annotations.text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems are sensitive to the ordering of retrieved documents, with language models exhibiting position bias that causes inconsistent outputs across different document permutations. We propose Citation-Consistent Voting (CCV), a training-free method that improves RAG robustness by aggregating answers based on document-ID agreement rather than answer frequency. CCV prompts the generator to cite supporting documents, maps citations to permutation-invariant document identifiers, and selects answers with the highest citation consistency across multiple permutations. On NaturalQuestions with Qwen3-8B and Contriever retrieval, CCV achieves 46.37% SubEM, outperforming majority voting by +0.19 points at K = 20 permutations. The improvement scales monotonically with the number of permutations, and diagnostic analysis confirms that citation agreement correlates significantly with answer correctness $( p = 1 . 1 4 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 } )$ . CCV requires no additional training and is compatible with any RAG system that can produce structured citations.
annotations.comment:
Page 1 - Abstract

Problem: The abstract claims a general, system-agnostic improvement (“compatible with any RAG system that can produce structured citations”), but the method as defined relies on (i) the model emitting stable doc indices/citations, and (ii) an “evidence-valid” filter that checks the *answer string appears in the quote* (a strong, format-specific assumption). This makes the applicability narrower than the current wording suggests.

Why it matters: Reviewers will interpret the abstract as promising broad applicability and robustness. If applicability is limited to extractive/substring-friendly answers (or to models that reliably follow a JSON-citation schema), the abstract overstates scope and may be judged as overclaiming.

Actionable fix (tighten scope + add key assumptions): Add one sentence stating the required citation interface and the two evidence-filter variants, and explicitly note that the strict quote constraint is optional and may reduce coverage.

Mentor Revised Version:
“Citation-Consistent Voting (CCV) is a training-free inference-time aggregator for permutation-ensembled RAG that selects answers whose *supporting document identity* is most consistent across retrieved-document permutations. CCV requires the generator to return a structured citation (document index plus an optional quote), maps indices to permutation-invariant document IDs, and optionally filters generations by a lightweight evidence check. On NaturalQuestions with Qwen3-8B and Contriever top-5 retrieval, CCV improves SubEM by 0.19 over answer-string majority voting at $K=20$ permutations, and citation-agreement scores correlate with correctness ($p=1.14\times10^{-5}$) under this evaluation setting.”
annotations.summary: Abstract overstates generality: CCV depends on structured citations and an evidence filter that may only suit extractive/substring-friendly answers. Tighten assumptions and scope in the abstract.

annotations.text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving the factual accuracy of large language models by grounding responses in retrieved documents (Gao et al., 2023). However, RAG systems exhibit a critical vulnerability: sensitivity to the ordering of retrieved documents. Liu et al. (2023) demonstrated the “lost in the middle” phenomenon, where models struggle to utilize information positioned in the middle of the context. More recently, Zhang et al. (2026) showed that even in short contexts with only five documents, merely permuting the document order can induce qualitatively different answers, including confident but incorrect responses.
annotations.comment:
Page 1 - Introduction (opening paragraph)

Problem: The introduction motivates permutation sensitivity mainly via “lost in the middle” and a cited Stable-RAG result, but it does not clarify *what exact threat model* you address: (i) position bias under long contexts, (ii) instability under *short* top-k contexts (top-5), or (iii) both. This matters because CCV’s mechanism (ensemble over permutations + aggregation) is primarily an inference-scaling strategy; readers will ask when it is worth the extra K passes.

Why it matters: Without a crisp threat model and a measurable definition of “permutation robustness” (e.g., variance of answer accuracy across permutations; probability of answer flip), it is hard to judge whether CCV solves a distinct problem beyond existing permutation ensembling/self-consistency lines of work.

Actionable fix: Add 2–3 sentences at the end of this paragraph defining (a) the setting (top-5 retrieval, short contexts), (b) the robustness metric you target (e.g., accuracy variance / flip rate across permutations), and (c) the practical deployment motivation for K-permutation inference.

Mentor Revised Version:
“In this paper we focus on *retrieval-permutation sensitivity* in short-context RAG: given a fixed top-$N$ retrieved set (we use $N=5$), different orderings of the same set can induce different final answers. We operationalize permutation robustness as the stability of the generated answer and its accuracy across random permutations (e.g., answer flip rate and accuracy variance across $K$ orderings). Our goal is to improve reliability in this setting using inference-time aggregation, without modifying model weights.”
annotations.summary: Clarify the paper’s threat model: short-context permutation sensitivity vs long-context position bias, and define the robustness metric (flip rate/variance) upfront.

annotations.text: Existing approaches to address this permutation sensitivity fall into two categories. Training-based methods like Stable-RAG (Zhang et al., 2026) use preference optimization to make generators invariant to document ordering, but require access to model weights and training data. Inference-time methods like Mixture-of-Agents (Wang et al., 2024) generate multiple responses under different document orderings and aggregate via majority voting, but this approach ignores the rich citation structure that modern RAG systems produce.
annotations.comment:
Page 1 - Introduction (prior work positioning paragraph)

Problem: The paragraph positions “majority vote over permutations” as the main inference-time baseline, but the related-work surface is likely incomplete for attribution/citation-based verification and for other order-invariance approaches. In particular, there are contemporaneous methods that (a) explicitly target permutation sensitivity (e.g., Stable-RAG [1]) and (b) aim for position/order-invariant RAG via inference-time KV-cache fusion [2]. Also, citation/attribution prompting is known to have format errors and hallucinated references; MIRAGE discusses these self-citation failure modes and proposes model-internal attribution [3]. None of these limitations/alternatives are acknowledged in this paragraph, which makes CCV’s novelty claim easier to dispute.

Why it matters: Reviewers will ask: “Is CCV just a heuristic variant of self-consistency/ensemble voting? Why should we trust self-citations?” Strong positioning requires explicitly stating what CCV adds beyond (i) majority vote, (ii) hidden-state clustering/decoding, and (iii) attribution systems.

Actionable fix: Add a short contrastive sentence per closest family:
- vs Stable-RAG: CCV is training-free and uses *document-ID agreement* as a signal, rather than clustering hidden states and decoding a cluster center.
- vs KV-Fusion: CCV does not change the model architecture or KV-cache handling; it trades compute (K passes) for robustness.
- vs MIRAGE/SAFE-like attribution: CCV uses citations as a *selection statistic*; attribution papers focus on *faithful explanation/grounding*, and they highlight citation-hallucination failure modes you must guard against.

Mentor Revised Version:
“Inference-time robustness can also be pursued via methods that directly model permutation sensitivity (e.g., Stable-RAG [1]) or modify inference to reduce order effects (e.g., KV-cache fusion for position-invariant RAG [2]). Separately, attribution work shows that self-citation prompting can be unreliable and proposes more faithful attribution mechanisms (e.g., MIRAGE [3]). CCV differs in that it is training-free and uses permutation-invariant document identities as an aggregation signal; however, it must also explicitly address citation/attribution failure modes discussed in this literature.”

References:
[1] Stable-RAG: Mitigating Retrieval-Permutation-Induced Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation 2601.02993

[2] Parallel Key-Value Cache Fusion for Position Invariant RAG 2501.07523

[3] Model Internals-based Answer Attribution for Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Generation 2406.13663
annotations.summary: Strengthen related-work positioning: cite/contrast permutation-robust and attribution-faithfulness methods, and acknowledge self-citation failure modes.

annotations.text: We observe that when language models cite evidence for their answers, the document they cite provides a more stable signal than the answer text itself. Our key insight is that correct answers tend to cite the same underlying document across permutations, while incorrect answers show more citation variance. This motivates a new aggregation strategy: rather than voting on answer frequency, we vote on document-ID agreement among evidence-valid responses.
annotations.comment:
Page 1 - Introduction (key insight paragraph)

Claim: “Correct answers tend to cite the same underlying document across permutations, while incorrect answers show more citation variance.”

Issue: This is a plausible hypothesis, but as written it reads like a general truth. It is also vulnerable to a correlated-failure counterexample: if retrieval contains a popular-but-wrong passage (or the model repeatedly latches onto the same misleading passage), then *wrong answers can also be citation-consistent*. In that case, maximizing doc-ID agreement may amplify systematic errors rather than fix them.

Why it matters: This is the core mechanism justification. If the signal is only weakly discriminative, the method may have limited value or require additional safeguards (e.g., incorporate doc quality/relevance or multi-document support).

Actionable fix: In the introduction, (i) explicitly frame this as an empirical hypothesis tested in Sec. 4.5, (ii) add one sentence acknowledging the correlated-failure case, and (iii) preview a mitigation/diagnostic you already compute (e.g., agreement-score calibration or combining agreement with an evidence-validity/coverage check).

Mentor Revised Version:
“We hypothesize—and test empirically in Sec. 4.5—that, conditioned on having at least one evidence-valid generation, correct answers exhibit higher *document-ID agreement* across permutations than incorrect ones. This signal is not foolproof: if multiple permutations consistently surface the same misleading passage, an incorrect answer may also appear citation-consistent. We therefore use agreement as an aggregation statistic alongside evidence-validity filtering and report diagnostic analyses that quantify when agreement is (and is not) predictive of correctness.”
annotations.summary: The core insight needs caveats: wrong answers can also be citation-consistent under correlated retrieval/model failures. Recast as tested hypothesis + add mitigation/diagnostic preview.

annotations.text: We propose Citation-Consistent Voting (CCV), a training-free method that aggregates answers based on document-ID agreement rather than answer frequency. CCV filters responses for evidence validity (ensuring the answer is grounded in the cited document), maps citations to permutation-invariant document IDs, and selects the answer with the highest citation-consistency score. Our contributions are:
annotations.comment:
Page 1 - Introduction (method summary + contributions paragraph)

Problem 1 (definition gap): The paragraph introduces “evidence validity” and “citation-consistency score” but does not state the exact definition until Sec. 3.2–3.3. For a short paper, readers benefit from a one-sentence formalization here (even informal) so they can understand what CCV optimizes.

Problem 2 (contribution framing): The contribution bullets mix method + a small absolute improvement (+0.19 SubEM) + a correlation test. Given the modest delta, reviewers will scrutinize whether the improvement is statistically reliable and whether the value is mainly diagnostic (the correlation signal) rather than a new algorithmic capability.

Actionable fix:
- Add one sentence with the score definition in words: “score(a) = number of evidence-valid runs citing the modal docID for answer a”.
- Reframe contributions so C2 emphasizes “robustness / stability improvement” and “where it helps” (unstable queries), not only the mean SubEM delta.
- Add an explicit note that the method targets *permutation robustness* rather than improving the underlying single-pass accuracy.

Mentor Revised Version:
“We propose CCV, which aggregates $K$ generations from different document permutations by selecting the answer whose supporting *document identity* is most consistent: for each answer string $a$, we count how many evidence-valid runs cite the modal underlying document ID for $a$, and choose the $a$ with the highest count. CCV is designed to improve permutation robustness (stability and accuracy under order perturbations) rather than to outperform the best single-pass prompt. Empirically, CCV yields small but consistent gains over answer-string majority voting on NaturalQuestions and primarily changes decisions on queries with high permutation instability.”
annotations.summary: Add a one-sentence definition of the CCV score and reframe contributions around permutation-robustness/stability (and where it helps), not only a small mean SubEM delta.

annotations.text: Large language models exhibit systematic biases in how they process information based on its position within the input context. Liu et al. (2023) demonstrated the “lost in the middle” phenomenon, where models perform best when relevant information appears at the beginning or end of the context, with significant performance degradation for information in the middle. This position sensitivity is particularly problematic for retrieval-augmented generation, where the ordering of retrieved documents can substantially affect answer quality. Our work addresses this challenge through inferencetime aggregation rather than architectural modifications.
annotations.comment:
Page 2 - Related Work (2.1 Position Bias in LMs paragraph)

Problem: The paragraph ends with “Our work addresses this challenge through inference-time aggregation,” which risks conflating *position bias in long contexts* with *permutation sensitivity under fixed top-$N$ short contexts*. You cite “lost in the middle”, but CCV’s experiments are in top-5 contexts; the reader needs an explicit bridge: why is permutation sensitivity the right operationalization of position bias here, and what is the relationship between the two?

Why it matters: Without this bridge, related work feels generic and the motivation chain weakens: the paper claims to fix a phenomenon (position bias) but evaluates another (permutation variance).

Actionable fix: Add one sentence defining the relationship: “Permutation sensitivity is an *instance* of position bias where relative ordering of equally retrieved evidence changes attention allocation; in short contexts this still appears as answer instability.” Also consider adding an empirical citation that studies order effects in RAG evaluation (e.g., retrieval robustness/order metric) to justify that order matters beyond long contexts.

Mentor Revised Version:
“While ‘lost in the middle’ is typically studied in long contexts, a related failure appears in short-context RAG: reordering a fixed top-$N$ retrieved set can shift attention and change the generated answer. We view this *retrieval-permutation sensitivity* as a practical instance of position bias, and we address it via inference-time aggregation across permutations rather than by modifying model architectures.”
annotations.summary: Related Work 2.1 needs a clearer bridge from long-context ‘lost in the middle’ to short-context retrieval-permutation sensitivity (the setting you actually evaluate).

annotations.text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances language model outputs by grounding responses in retrieved documents (Gao et al., 2023). Dense retrieval methods such as DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020) and Contriever (Izacard et al., 2021) have enabled effective passage retrieval for open-domain question answering. However, RAG systems inherit the position biases of their underlying language models, making them sensitive to the ordering of retrieved documents. Recent work has explored various strategies to improve RAG robustness, including training-based approaches (Zhang et al., 2026) and inference-time methods (Lee et al., 2024).
annotations.comment:
Page 2 - Related Work (2.2 RAG paragraph)

Problem: The paragraph lists retrievers and then says “Recent work … training-based (Zhang et al., 2026) and inference-time (Lee et al., 2024)”, but it does not categorize *what* these methods do along the axis relevant to CCV (order-invariance / permutation-robustness). This makes the related work read like a generic RAG overview rather than a targeted positioning.

Why it matters: CCV’s novelty/value is about permutation robustness and aggregation signals. The related-work section should quickly teach the reader the existing solution space: (i) make model less order-sensitive, (ii) aggregate multiple runs, (iii) improve citation/attribution faithfulness, (iv) retrieval-side fixes.

Actionable fix: Rewrite 2.2 as a short taxonomy paragraph with 2–3 buckets, and place CCV explicitly as “inference-time multi-permutation aggregation using citation/document-ID consistency”. Also, if you keep Lee et al. (2024) as an ‘inference scaling’ citation, add one sentence explaining how that relates (or does not relate) to permutation robustness.

Mentor Revised Version:
“Prior work on robust RAG spans (i) *model-side* methods that reduce order sensitivity via training or inference modifications, (ii) *inference-time ensembling* that aggregates multiple generations to mitigate instability, and (iii) *attribution/grounding* methods that improve faithfulness of evidence citations. CCV sits in category (ii) but differs from answer-string voting by using permutation-invariant document identities as the aggregation signal, which is complementary to model-side invariance and to attribution-faithfulness improvements.”
annotations.summary: Rewrite Related Work 2.2 into a targeted taxonomy aligned with CCV’s permutation-robustness contribution instead of a generic RAG overview.

annotations.text: Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) improves chain-of-thought reasoning by sampling multiple reasoning paths and selecting the most consistent answer through majority voting. This principle has been extended to multi-agent systems, where Mixture-of-Agents (Wang et al., 2024) aggregates outputs from multiple language models to improve response quality. Tang et al. (2023) applied permutation self-consistency to listwise ranking, demonstrating that aggregating predictions across different input orderings can mitigate position bias. Our citation-consistent voting extends this paradigm by using document citations rather than answer frequency as the aggregation signal.
annotations.comment:
Page 2 - Related Work (2.3 Self-consistency / ensemble paragraph)

Problem: You correctly cite self-consistency/majority voting, but you do not explicitly justify why *answer-string* majority voting is the wrong statistic in RAG, nor do you compare CCV to other non-majority aggregation rules (e.g., ranked voting variants, confidence-weighting, or marginal-based methods). Given your paper’s core claim is “vote on evidence not answers,” this paragraph should articulate the failure mode: semantically equivalent answers may have different strings; or incorrect answers may be frequent due to shared bias.

Why it matters: This is where the reader should be convinced that CCV is not just “another voting heuristic” but a motivated shift in aggregation signal.

Actionable fix: Add a short diagnostic example (one sentence) and a one-sentence theoretical intuition: “answer strings are not permutation-invariant and have high surface entropy; docIDs are permutation-invariant under mapping.” Also cite one recent work that improves self-consistency via richer voting (e.g., ranked voting self-consistency) as a foil to motivate CCV’s alternative.

Mentor Revised Version:
“In RAG, majority voting over answer strings is brittle because equivalent answers may appear with different surface forms, while biased retrieval can make an incorrect answer frequent. CCV changes the aggregation statistic from surface form to *evidence identity*: after mapping citations to permutation-invariant document IDs, agreement becomes comparable across permutations even when answer strings vary. This is complementary to richer self-consistency rules (e.g., ranked-voting self-consistency) that still operate on answers rather than evidence.”
annotations.summary: Strengthen the argument why answer-string majority vote is the wrong statistic in RAG; add intuition/example and position CCV against richer self-consistency voting baselines.

annotations.text: Several approaches have been proposed to address permutation sensitivity in RAG systems. Stable-RAG (Zhang et al., 2026) uses preference optimization to train models that produce consistent outputs regardless of document ordering, but requires access to model weights and training data. Tang et al. (2023) proposed permutation self-consistency for ranking tasks, aggregating predictions across multiple orderings. Our approach differs by exploiting the citation structure in model outputs, using document-ID agreement rather than answer frequency for aggregation, and requiring no training.
annotations.comment:
Page 2 - Related Work (2.4 Permutation-robust RAG paragraph)

Problem: This paragraph is closest to CCV’s core topic but still underspecifies the comparison axis. You mention Stable-RAG and permutation self-consistency for ranking, then state “Our approach differs by exploiting citation structure.” This is directionally correct, but reviewers will want a sharper “overlap vs residual novelty” statement:
- Stable-RAG explicitly targets retrieval-permutation-induced hallucinations; CCV also uses multiple permutations. So the novelty cannot be “we use permutations” but must be “we use *document-ID agreement via citations* as a training-free selector.”
- The paragraph does not acknowledge that citation prompting may be unreliable (format errors / citing non-existent sources), which is relevant here and discussed in attribution literature.

Why it matters: Novelty and defensibility hinge on clean differentiation and on acknowledging failure modes of the proposed signal.

Actionable fix: Expand this paragraph by ~3–4 sentences:
(1) one sentence describing Stable-RAG’s core mechanism at a high level (hidden-state clustering / cluster-center decoding) and contrasting with CCV;
(2) one sentence describing the reliability risk of self-citations and how CCV mitigates it (evidence-validity filter, or plans for better attribution);
(3) one sentence clarifying that CCV is training-free and thus targets a different deployment constraint.

Mentor Revised Version:
“Stable-RAG [1] addresses permutation-induced hallucinations by aggregating internal representations across permutations (e.g., clustering hidden states and decoding from a dominant cluster center), requiring model-internal access and/or additional machinery beyond simple voting. In contrast, CCV is training-free and uses an externally observable signal—permutation-invariant document IDs obtained from model-produced citations—to select among $K$ generations. Because self-citations can be unreliable, CCV must explicitly validate or calibrate citations (we use an evidence-validity filter and report coverage/diagnostics), and future work can integrate more faithful attribution methods.”

References:
[1] Stable-RAG: Mitigating Retrieval-Permutation-Induced Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation 2601.02993
annotations.summary: Sharpen the Stable-RAG vs CCV comparison and explicitly acknowledge citation unreliability as a core risk for a citation-based selector.

annotations.text: Consider a query q and a set of N retrieved documents $\mathcal { D } = \{ d _ { 1 } , \ldots , d _ { N } \}$ . Standard RAG generates a single response by conditioning on a fixed ordering of D. However, the generator’s output can vary significantly depending on document order due to position bias (Liu et al., 2023). Multi-permutation RAG addresses this by sampling K random permutations $\pi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pi _ { K }$ of the document indices and generating K responses, one for each ordering. The challenge is then to aggregate these K responses into a single, more reliable answer.
annotations.comment:
Page 3 - Method (3.1 Problem Setup paragraph)

Problem: The setup introduces multi-permutation RAG and says “the challenge is to aggregate these K responses,” but it does not specify whether K permutations are sampled with replacement, whether the retrieved set is fixed per query, and whether the same retrieved set is used for all permutations (implied) versus re-retrieval. These details matter for reproducibility and for interpreting the robustness claim.

Why it matters: If the retrieved documents differ across runs (query-time nondeterminism, retrieval randomness), then “permutation robustness” becomes conflated with “retrieval robustness”. Your method assumes a fixed set where only order changes.

Actionable fix: Add 2–3 explicit assumptions:
- retrieval is deterministic and the top-$N$ set is fixed per query;
- you sample K random permutations *without replacement* over the same set (or specify if with replacement);
- define a robustness metric (answer flip rate / variance) in this section so the method has a clear optimization target.

Mentor Revised Version:
“For each query, we fix the retrieved top-$N$ document set $\mathcal{D}$ (using a deterministic retriever configuration) and generate $K$ answers by sampling $K$ random permutations of the same set (report whether sampling is with/without replacement). Our goal is to improve *permutation robustness*—measured by answer stability and accuracy across these orderings—by selecting a single final answer from the $K$ generations.”
annotations.summary: Clarify key setup assumptions (fixed retrieved set, permutation sampling scheme) to avoid conflating permutation sensitivity with retrieval randomness; define robustness metric here.

annotations.text:
We prompt the generator to produce structured outputs containing an answer, a document index, and a supporting quote. Specifically, each response $r _ { k }$ for permutation $\pi _ { k }$ contains: (1) an answer string $a _ { k } , ( 2 )$ a document index $j _ { k } \in \{ 1 , \ldots , \bar { N } \}$ indicating which document in the permuted order supports the answer, and (3) a quote $e _ { k }$ extracted from that document.
A response is considered evidence-valid if it satisfies two criteria. First, the cited document index must be valid $( j _ { k } \in \{ 1 , \ldots , N \} )$ . Second, the answer must be grounded in the cited document, which we verify by checking that the quote $e _ { k }$ appears in document $d _ { \pi _ { k } ( j _ { k } ) }$ and that the answer $a _ { k }$ appears in the quote $e _ { k }$ . Responses failing these checks are filtered out before aggregation.
annotations.comment:
Page 3 - Method (3.2 Evidence Filtering paragraph)

Problem 1 (overly strict / potentially misaligned “evidence-valid” test): The filter requires (a) the quote substring exists in the cited document and (b) the *answer string appears in the quote*. This is effectively an extractive constraint; it will reject many correct but abstractive answers (e.g., normalized entities, multi-token variants, date formats), and it can be gamed by the model copying the answer into any quote-like span.

Problem 2 (terminology/notation inconsistency): You introduce $j_k \in \{1,\ldots,\bar N\}$ but later validate $j_k \in \{1,\ldots,N\}$. The meaning of $\bar N$ is not defined, and this creates avoidable confusion about index ranges.

Why it matters: Since CCV’s scores count only “evidence-valid” responses, the filter definition affects both (i) coverage and (ii) which answers win. A too-strict filter can bias results and reduce generality; an easily gamed filter can inflate “validity” without true grounding.

Actionable fixes:
1) Replace “answer appears in quote” with a more robust entailment-style check, or at least a normalization-aware match:
   - For entity answers: case-folding + punctuation stripping + alias matching.
   - For numeric/date answers: canonicalization rules.
   - For multi-token answers: allow partial match with high overlap.
   If you want to stay training-free, you can implement lightweight normalization plus a fuzzy match threshold.
2) Define the index domain cleanly and remove $\bar N$ unless needed.
3) Report how often this filter rejects otherwise plausible answers and whether rejection correlates with correctness.

Mentor Revised Version:
“A response is evidence-valid if it cites an in-range document index $j_k\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ and provides a quote string $e_k$ that occurs in the cited document. To avoid restricting to purely extractive answers, we check grounding using a lightweight normalization-aware match between the predicted answer and the cited quote (e.g., canonicalizing case/punctuation and normalizing numbers/dates), and we report the resulting valid-run coverage and rejection analysis.”
annotations.summary: The current evidence-validity filter is extractive (answer must appear in quote) and has notation inconsistency ($\bar N$ vs $N$). Use normalization-aware grounding checks and clean index definitions.

annotations.text:
The key insight of CCV is that correct answers tend to cite the same underlying document across permutations, while incorrect answers show more citation variance. We exploit this by aggregating based on document-ID agreement rather than answer frequency.
For each permutation $\pi _ { k }$ , we map the cited document index $j _ { k }$ to an underlying document ID that is invariant to permutation: $\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { l o c I D } ( r _ { k } ) = \pi _ { k } ( j _ { k } ) } \end{array}$ . This mapping ensures that citations to the same document are recognized as such regardless of where that document appeared in the permuted order.
annotations.comment:
Page 3 - Method (3.3 Citation-consistent aggregation paragraph)

Problem 1 (notation bug / clarity): You define the mapping as $\mathrm{locID}(r_k)=\pi_k(j_k)$, but the rest of the section uses $\operatorname{docID}(r)$. This looks like a typo/inconsistency (locID vs docID). It becomes more confusing because docID is the *underlying* permutation-invariant identifier.

Problem 2 (tie-breaking and answer equivalence): The algorithm groups by “unique answer a” and tie-breaks by raw answer frequency. But in QA, semantically identical answers often differ in surface form (“Barack Obama” vs “Obama”; “United States” vs “USA”), so grouping by raw string can fracture votes and degrade CCV. In the worst case, CCV might select a less canonical alias purely due to string variance.

Why it matters: This is the core algorithm definition. If docID mapping is unclear or answer canonicalization is missing, the method becomes brittle and hard to reproduce.

Actionable fixes:
1) Use one identifier name consistently. For example: define $\operatorname{docID}(r_k)=\pi_k(j_k)$ and use docID everywhere.
2) Add an answer normalization step before grouping (lowercasing, punctuation stripping, common alias rules), or compute equivalence classes via simple heuristics (e.g., whitespace token set overlap) since you want training-free.
3) Report how often normalization merges answers and whether it changes winners.

Mentor Revised Version:
“For each evidence-valid response $r_k$, we map its cited index to a permutation-invariant identifier via $\operatorname{docID}(r_k)=\pi_k(j_k)$. We then normalize answer strings (case/punctuation/alias rules) and group responses by the normalized answer. CCV selects the answer with the largest within-group agreement on the modal $\operatorname{docID}$, and uses (normalized) answer frequency only as a secondary tie-break.”
annotations.summary: Fix docID/locID inconsistency and add answer normalization before grouping; otherwise CCV is brittle to paraphrases/aliases and hard to reproduce.

annotations.text:
Quote Constraint Relaxation. The strict quote verification (requiring exact substring match) can reduce citation path coverage when models produce paraphrased or slightly modified quotes. We find that relaxing this constraint to only require valid document index (without quote verification) improves coverage while maintaining the benefit of document-ID agreement. We evaluate both variants in our experiments.
Computational Cost. CCV requires K forward passes through the generator, the same as standard multi-permutation approaches like Mixture-of-Agents (Wang et al., 2024). The additional overhead of evidence filtering and citation-consistent aggregation is negligible compared to generation cost. The method is compatible with batched inference and can leverage KV-cache sharing across permutations that share document prefixes.
annotations.comment:
Page 4 - Method/Experiments boundary (3.4 Practical considerations + 4.1 Setup)

Issue: The paper claims CCV is “compatible with any RAG system that can produce structured citations,” yet the practical-considerations section already reveals non-trivial engineering assumptions (JSON-constrained output, quote extraction behavior, possible KV-cache sharing across permutations). The experimental setup also fixes decoding to greedy with temperature=0, which reduces output diversity and may understate/overstate the need for voting depending on model.

Why it matters: Reproducibility and external validity. Readers need to know whether CCV’s gains persist under:
- non-greedy decoding (temperature > 0),
- different generators/retrievers,
- larger $N$ (top-20),
- contexts where answers are not strict substrings.

Actionable fix: Expand 4.1 to include: exact prompt template (JSON schema), how quotes are extracted, how permutations are sampled, and whether generation is deterministic. Add at least one robustness run varying temperature (e.g., 0 vs 0.2) to show CCV is not an artifact of greedy decoding.

Mentor Revised Version:
“We use a JSON-constrained prompt that requires {answer, doc_idx, quote} outputs; Appendix A lists the exact template. Unless otherwise stated, retrieval is deterministic and we sample $K$ random permutations of the same top-$N$ set per query. We report results under greedy decoding (T=0) and a low-temperature setting (e.g., T=0.2) to assess whether CCV’s citation-consistency signal remains predictive when answer strings become more diverse.”
annotations.summary: Expand experimental setup for reproducibility (prompt/schema, permutation sampling, determinism) and add a decoding-robustness check (T=0 vs >0) since voting behavior depends on output diversity.

annotations.text: Table 1 presents the main results. Citation-consistent voting achieves 46.37% SubEM and 46.83% F1 at $K = 2 0$ , outperforming MoA majority voting by +0.19 SubEM and +0.17 F1. The improvement is consistent across both metrics, demonstrating that document-ID agreement provides a more reliable aggregation signal than answer frequency alone. We note that the standard Vanilla RAG prompt achieves higher SubEM (48.98%) but lower F1 (41.10%) compared to the JSON citation prompt, reflecting differences in output format rather than method quality. Among methods using the same JSON citation format, multi-permutation approaches consistently outperform single-pass generation.
annotations.comment:
Page 4 - Experiments (4.2 Main results paragraph)

Numerical/claim audit (F1/F2): You argue CCV “outperforms MoA majority voting by +0.19 SubEM and +0.17 F1” and then note that Vanilla RAG (standard prompt) has higher SubEM but lower F1 than the JSON-citation prompt, attributing this to “differences in output format rather than method quality.” This is plausible, but it is currently asserted without evidence.

Why it matters: The biggest headline is only +0.19 SubEM. If the evaluation metric is sensitive to formatting (and SubEM is substring-based), then small deltas can be artifacts of answer formatting/canonicalization rather than real correctness changes. Also, the claim that the prompt-format difference is not “method quality” needs substantiation.

Actionable fixes:
1) Report canonicalization rules used before computing SubEM/F1 for each prompt type (e.g., lowercasing, punctuation stripping, article removal). If none, add them.
2) Add an error analysis: show examples where JSON citation prompt changes answer surface form causing SubEM drop but F1 rise.
3) Add a statistical test (paired bootstrap) for the +0.19 improvement, or at least multi-seed retrieval/permutation sampling variance, since Table 1 mixes a ± value for K=5 but not for K=20.

Mentor Revised Version:
“To ensure the small gains are not formatting artifacts, we apply identical answer normalization for all methods before computing SubEM/F1 and report the normalization rules. We additionally run a paired bootstrap test over queries for CCV vs majority vote at $K=20$ and provide a brief qualitative analysis of cases where the JSON citation prompt changes answer surface forms (affecting SubEM vs F1 differently).”
annotations.summary: Given the +0.19 SubEM headline and SubEM’s format sensitivity, you must report answer-normalization and statistical reliability; otherwise improvements may be formatting artifacts.

annotations.text: Figure 2 and Table 2 show how the improvement of citation-consistent voting over majority voting scales with the number of permutations. At K = 5, the two methods perform nearly identically $( \Delta = - 0 . 0 1 )$ , but as K increases, citation-consistent voting shows monotonically increasing gains: +0.10 at K = 10, +0.11 at K = 15, and +0.19 at K = 20. This scaling behavior suggests that more permutations provide more reliable citation agreement signals, as the document-ID voting mechanism benefits from a larger sample of evidence-valid responses to identify consistent citation patterns.
annotations.comment:
Page 5 - Experiments (4.3 K-scaling analysis paragraph)

Problem: You claim monotonic scaling of the improvement with K and interpret it as evidence that “more permutations provide more reliable citation agreement signals.” Two concerns:

(1) Monotonicity is shown only on one dataset/model pair and with small deltas (0.10–0.19). Without confidence intervals across multiple random permutation samples and/or retriever randomness, “monotonic” may be within noise.

(2) The interpretation is one-directional; an alternative explanation is that larger K increases the chance of “finding” a correct answer at least once (a standard inference-scaling effect), and then any selector (including majority vote) improves. To claim the *signal* improves with K, you should show that citation-agreement discriminability (e.g., AUC for correctness vs agreement score) increases with K, not only SubEM.

Why it matters: This paragraph is doing causal interpretation (“agreement becomes more reliable with K”). It should be supported by signal-level diagnostics and uncertainty reporting.

Actionable fix:
- Report variance/CI of SubEM for each K using multiple random seeds for permutation sampling.
- Add a plot/table of agreement-score distributions for correct vs incorrect predictions at each K (or an AUC/KS statistic) to directly support the ‘signal reliability’ claim.

Mentor Revised Version:
“Across $K\in\{5,10,15,20\}$ we observe small improvements of CCV over majority voting. To assess whether gains are robust, we repeat permutation sampling with multiple random seeds and report mean±CI for each K. We also measure how well the citation-agreement score separates correct from incorrect predictions at each K (e.g., AUC), which more directly tests whether agreement becomes a better quality signal as K grows.”
annotations.summary: The ‘monotonic with K’ claim needs uncertainty (multi-seed permutation sampling) and signal-level diagnostics (agreement-score separability vs correctness) to justify the interpretation.

annotations.text:
To validate the core hypothesis that citation agreement correlates with answer correctness, we analyze the relationship between document-ID agreement scores and prediction accuracy. Correct predictions have significantly higher mean agreement scores than incorrect ones (3.04 vs. 2.85, Mann-Whitney $p \ = \ 1 . 1 4 \times \mathrm { \bar { 1 0 ^ { - 5 } } } ,$ , confirming that citation consistency is a meaningful quality signal.
We further examine where citation-consistent voting differs from majority voting. The method primarily acts on unstable queries, defined as those producing three or more unique answers across permutations. Among the 699 unstable queries (19.4% of the test set), citation-consistent voting selects a different answer than majority voting in 19.89% of cases. This targeted behavior confirms that the method intervenes precisely where frequency-based voting is least reliable, while leaving stable queries unchanged.
annotations.comment:
Page 6 - Experiments (4.5 Diagnostic analysis paragraph)

Problem: You report a significant difference in mean agreement scores (3.04 vs 2.85) with a Mann–Whitney $p$-value, and then use this to support “citation consistency is meaningful.” Statistical significance is expected with large n (3,610 queries), but the effect size is small. The paper does not report an effect size (e.g., rank-biserial correlation / Cliff’s delta) or an operational threshold showing how agreement would be used to *predict* correctness.

Why it matters: The diagnostic claim is one of the three listed contributions. Reviewers will ask: “Is this practically useful, or only statistically detectable?” Without effect size, it is hard to assess practical value.

Actionable fix:
- Report effect size and confidence intervals.
- Add a simple calibration: e.g., correctness rate vs agreement score (bucketed), or an ROC/AUC for agreement predicting correctness.
- Fix the apparent LaTeX/typo in the $p$-value rendering (it appears corrupted elsewhere in the PDF).

Mentor Revised Version:
“Correct predictions show slightly higher agreement scores than incorrect ones (3.04 vs 2.85; Mann–Whitney $p=1.14\times 10^{-5}$). To quantify practical usefulness, we additionally report an effect size (e.g., Cliff’s $\delta$ with CI) and plot accuracy as a function of agreement score (or AUC for agreement predicting correctness). We also correct the $p$-value rendering for consistent presentation.”
annotations.summary: Diagnostic analysis needs effect size and calibration (accuracy vs agreement/AUC), not only a p-value; significance alone is not informative at n≈3.6k.

annotations.text:
We presented Citation-Consistent Voting, a training-free method for improving RAG robustness by aggregating answers based on document-ID agreement rather than answer frequency. On NaturalQuestions, CCV achieves +0.19 SubEM improvement over majority voting at $K = 2 0$ permutations, with gains scaling monotonically with K. Diagnostic analysis confirms that citation agreement correlates significantly with answer correctness $( \bar { p } = 1 . 1 4 \times \mathrm { { i } 0 ^ { - 5 } ) }$ .
Our work has several limitations. The improvement, while consistent, is modest in absolute terms. Evaluation is limited to a single dataset and model. The method requires K forward passes, adding computational cost. Future work could explore combining CCV with training-based approaches like Stable-RAG (Zhang et al., 2026), evaluating on additional datasets, and investigating other citation signals beyond document-ID agreement.
annotations.comment:
Page 6 - Conclusion

Problem: The conclusion repeats the main performance and correlation claims, but it does not clearly restate the scope limits that the paper actually demonstrates: single dataset (NQ), single retriever (Contriever), single generator (Qwen3-8B), and a small absolute delta. It also mentions combining with Stable-RAG as future work but does not articulate a crisp “when to use CCV” recommendation given compute cost.

Why it matters: A defensible conclusion should help the reader form the correct belief: CCV is a lightweight selector that can improve reliability for unstable queries, but it is not a universal accuracy booster and has costs.

Actionable fix: Rewrite the conclusion into (i) validated claim (scoped), (ii) practical guidance (compute vs gain; unstable-query targeting), (iii) prioritized next experiments (multi-dataset, temperature, retriever variance).

Mentor Revised Version:
“In the evaluated setting (NaturalQuestions; Contriever top-5; Qwen3-8B; greedy decoding), CCV provides a small but consistent improvement over answer-string majority voting by selecting answers whose cited document identity is most consistent across retrieval permutations. The method is most relevant for queries that exhibit high permutation instability; in stable cases it typically matches majority voting while still incurring $K$ forward passes. Future work should test CCV across additional datasets/models/retrievers, report statistical reliability under repeated permutation sampling, and explore hybrid designs that combine CCV’s citation-based selection with model-side permutation-robust methods such as Stable-RAG.”
annotations.summary: Conclusion should more explicitly bound claims (single dataset/model, small delta) and give practical guidance (when to use CCV given K-pass cost) plus a prioritized next-experiment list.

annotations.text: Table 3 compares citation-consistent voting with and without the verbatim quote constraint at $K = 5$ . Requiring exact quote matches reduces citation path coverage to 96.37% (the fraction of queries with at least one evidence-valid response) and yields only 4.12 valid runs per query on average. Relaxing this constraint to only require valid document indices increases coverage to 99.70% and valid runs to 4.96, resulting in a substantial improvement from 45.73% to 46.37%
annotations.comment:
Page 5 - Experiments (4.4 Quote-constraint ablation paragraph)

F1/F2 consistency issue + interpretation gap: This paragraph states that relaxing the quote constraint improves SubEM from 45.73% to 46.37% “(SubEM +0.64)” at $K=5$. But elsewhere, CCV’s main result 46.37% is reported at $K=20$. As written, a reader can easily misinterpret which K each number corresponds to, and whether 46.37 at K=5 is consistent with Table 2 (which reports ~45.81 at K=5 for citation voting).

Why it matters: This is a numerical-clarity/reliability issue. Given that the paper’s overall gains are small, any ambiguity about which setting produced 46.37% undermines trust.

Actionable fixes:
1) Make K explicit in the sentence that reports 46.37% (e.g., “at K=5 (no quote) SubEM=XX”).
2) Ensure all K-dependent numbers are consistent across Table 1/2/3 and the narrative.
3) If 46.37% at K=5 is a different evaluation variant than Table 2 (e.g., different filtering definition), explicitly label it as such.

Mentor Revised Version:
“At $K=5$, enforcing exact quote matching reduces the fraction of queries with at least one evidence-valid run to 96.37% and yields 4.12 valid runs/query. Relaxing the quote check (keeping only in-range doc indices) increases coverage to 99.70% and 4.96 valid runs/query, improving SubEM by +0.64 *under this $K=5$ setting*. Please ensure that the reported SubEM values for $K=5$ align with Table 2 (or clearly state if this ablation uses a different evaluation variant than the K-scaling table).”
annotations.summary: Clarify and reconcile K-dependent SubEM numbers in the quote-constraint ablation; current text risks inconsistency (46.37 at K=5 vs main 46.37 at K=20 / Table 2).

annotations.text:
For each unique answer a, let R(a) denote the set of evidence-valid responses producing answer a. We compute the modal document ID among these responses:
$$
\operatorname{doc} ^ {*} (a) = \arg \max _ {d} | \{r \in R (a): \operatorname{docID} (r) = d \} | \tag {1}
$$
The citation-consistency score for answer a is then defined as the number of evidence-valid responses that cite this modal document:
$$
\operatorname{score} (a) = \left| \left\{r \in R (a): \operatorname{docID} (r) = \operatorname{doc} ^ {*} (a) \right\} \right| \tag {2}
$$
The final answer is selected as arg maxa score(a), with ties broken by raw answer frequency across all K runs.
annotations.comment:
Page 4 - Method (Eq. 1–2 definition block)

Problem 1 (undefined edge cases): Eq. (1)–(2) assume each candidate answer $a$ has at least one evidence-valid response $R(a)\neq\emptyset$. In practice, you can have queries where *no* run passes evidence filtering (especially under strict quote checks). The paper does not specify the fallback rule, so the algorithm is not fully defined.

Problem 2 (argmax domain + tie handling): In Eq. (1), the domain of $d$ is not stated (is it $d\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ doc IDs, or arbitrary identifiers?). Also, ties for $\operatorname{doc}^*(a)$ and ties for $\operatorname{score}(a)$ are not fully specified (you mention tie-breaking by answer frequency for the final selection, but not for $\operatorname{doc}^*$).

Why it matters: These are “silent” implementation choices that can materially change results when improvements are small (+0.19). Reviewers will flag missing edge-case definitions as a reproducibility gap.

Actionable fix: Add a short algorithm box or 4–5 lines of text that fully defines:
- docID domain: $\operatorname{docID}(r_k)=\pi_k(j_k)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$
- what to do if all runs are filtered out (e.g., fall back to majority vote over all K runs, or drop the evidence filter and recompute scores)
- tie-breaking for $\operatorname{doc}^*(a)$ and $\operatorname{score}(a)$
- (optional but recommended) answer normalization before defining “unique answer a”.

Mentor Revised Version:
“We define $\operatorname{docID}(r_k)=\pi_k(j_k)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ for each evidence-valid response. For each normalized answer $a$, let $R(a)$ be the set of valid responses with that answer; if $R(a)=\emptyset$ for all $a$, we fall back to answer-string majority voting over all $K$ runs. Otherwise, we set $\operatorname{doc}^*(a)=\arg\max_{d\in\{1,\ldots,N\}} |\{r\in R(a):\operatorname{docID}(r)=d\}|$ (breaking ties by global frequency), compute $\operatorname{score}(a)=|\{r\in R(a):\operatorname{docID}(r)=\operatorname{doc}^*(a)\}|$, and select the $a$ with maximum score (breaking ties by normalized answer frequency).”
annotations.summary: Define edge cases and tie-breaking for Eq. (1)–(2): what if no evidence-valid runs exist, what is the argmax domain, and how doc*/score ties are resolved.

annotations.text:
We evaluate Citation-Consistent Voting on the NaturalQuestions (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019) opendomain QA benchmark, using 3,610 test queries. For retrieval, we use Contriever (Izacard et al., 2021) to retrieve the top-5 passages from Wikipedia. The generator is Qwen3-8B with greedy decoding (temperature=0). We report Substring Exact Match (SubEM), where a prediction is correct if the gold answer appears as a substring, and token-level F1 score.
We compare against two baselines. Vanilla RAG generates a single response without permutation ensembling. MoA Majority Vote (Wang et al., 2024) generates K responses under different document orderings and selects the most frequent answer. For multi-permutation methods, we evaluate at $K \in \{ 5 , 1 0 , 1 5 , 2 0 \}$ permutations.
annotations.comment:
Page 4 - Experiments (4.1 Experimental setup paragraphs)

Problem: The setup provides high-level choices (dataset size, retriever, generator, greedy decoding, metrics) but is missing several reproducibility-critical details that directly affect small deltas:
- Exact NaturalQuestions split/version and any preprocessing (answer aliases, punctuation/case normalization).
- Prompt template / JSON schema and any constrained decoding (and how often formatting fails).
- How permutations are sampled (random seed; with/without replacement) and whether retrieval is deterministic.
- Whether the retriever corpus is Wikipedia snapshots consistent with NQ, and how passages are chunked.
- Hardware/latency for $K\in\{5,10,15,20\}$ so readers can judge the compute–gain trade-off.

Why it matters: With +0.19 SubEM headline improvements, even minor implementation differences (normalization, prompt constraints, random seeds) can change outcomes. Missing details reduce confidence and make it hard for others to adopt CCV.

Actionable fix: Add an “Implementation Details” paragraph (or appendix) that fully specifies the above, and report (i) citation/JSON validity rate and (ii) evidence-valid coverage rate under each filter.

Mentor Revised Version:
“We use the NaturalQuestions open-domain QA test set of 3,610 queries (specify exact split/version) with a fixed Wikipedia snapshot and passage chunking scheme (report chunk size/overlap). For each query we retrieve a deterministic top-$N$ set and sample $K$ random permutations with a fixed RNG seed (state whether sampling is with/without replacement). The generator is prompted with a JSON schema (Appendix A lists the exact template) and decoding constraints; we report schema-valid rate and evidence-valid coverage. All answers are normalized with the same rules before computing SubEM/F1 (list rules). We additionally report wall-clock cost for each $K$ to quantify the compute–robustness trade-off.”
annotations.summary: Add missing reproducibility details in 4.1 (prompt/schema, permutation sampling, normalization, seeds, corpus/chunking, compute). Small reported gains need tight experimental specification.
